claims.text: This is a from-scratch bakery-style cafe that bakes its own bread and sourdough on site and serves toasts, muffins and cookies, so wheat flour is heavily present in the kitchen. No gluten-free preparation or cross-contamination protocols are documented in any source. Celiac diners should treat the cafe as not verified celiac-safe and confirm options directly with staff before ordering.

This is a vegetarian cafe rather than an all-vegan kitchen. Reviewers note the sandwiches are vegan (including the bread), several items can be ordered vegan, but some toasts contain cheese and are vegetarian only. Dairy is present in the kitchen, so strict vegans should specify a vegan order and confirm there is no cross-contact.
The listing states the cafe offers vegan and egg-free menu options.
The cafe has a clearly marked vegan and egg-free menu, and sandwiches including the bread are vegan, with several other items available made vegan on request.
Food is made from scratch with no pre-packaged ingredients, and reviewers consistently praise the freshness of the tofu sandwiches, guacamole toast and baked goods.

This is not a celiac-safe restaurant. The kitchen openly works with wheat-based ingredients — nama-fu (fresh wheat-gluten cake) is a featured ingredient — so gluten is present throughout the cooking, and there is no indication of separate gluten-free preparation.
The set menu is fixed and changes daily, with no published gluten-free option, so a celiac diner cannot rely on a safe alternative being available.

The cooking is built on traditional Japanese dashi and seasoning, and the signature yuba donburi uses a Japanese-style ankake sauce. Standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so these dishes should be assumed to contain wheat-based soy sauce unless the kitchen confirms otherwise.

hale is a fully vegetarian/vegan kitchen with no animal products used, which greatly reduces the risk of animal cross-contact for vegan diners. The dashi is plant-based (kombu) rather than fish-based.
The entire menu is vegan/vegetarian with no animal products, so vegan diners can order freely without parsing ingredients.
The owner emphasizes safe, local, pesticide-free ingredients sourced from trusted Kyoto suppliers, reflecting genuine care about what goes into the food.

CoCo Ichibanya offers an allergen-free curry that uses none of Japan's 7 major allergens (egg, dairy, wheat, buckwheat, peanut, shrimp, crab). To limit cross-contamination, the curry sauce is brought to the table sealed in an unopened retort pouch that you open yourself, rather than being plated from shared kitchen containers.

The company openly states that contamination can occur both in the factory and in-store through shared equipment, utensils, and hand contact during cooking. The standard menu is not prepared in a celiac-safe environment.
The allergen-free curry is not certified as a medical or special-purpose food, and not every branch stocks it. Confirm availability at this Enmachi location before relying on it.

The standard Japanese curry roux is wheat-thickened, and most Japanese soy sauce used in seasonings contains wheat. The regular curry sauce is therefore not gluten-free; only the dedicated sealed allergen-free pouch is formulated without wheat.

An animal-ingredient-free version of the allergen-free curry is reported to exist, which can suit vegan diners. However, it is prepared in a kitchen that handles meat, seafood, dairy, and egg, so trace cross-contact is possible.
For the allergen-free curry, staff serve the sauce in its sealed pouch and provide a disposable plastic spoon instead of a shared metal utensil, reducing secondary cross-contact.
Detailed per-item allergen and nutrition charts are published on the official site, so you can check specific ingredients before ordering or show staff your requirements.
The sealed, unopened allergen-free curry pouch is one of the more reassuring fast-curry options in Japan for avoiding the 7 major allergens, since the sauce never touches shared serving equipment.
Convenient location near Enmachi for visits to Nijo Castle and the Kinkaku-ji / Kitano-Tenmangu area, open daily with long hours.

CoCo Ichibanya offers a dedicated curry made without the seven specified allergens (egg, dairy, wheat, buckwheat, peanut, shrimp, crab). To reduce the risk of cross-contact in the kitchen, this allergen-free curry sauce is served sealed in its original retail pouch rather than plated from the regular line.
The company notes this allergen-free curry is not an officially certified medical food, so celiac diners should treat it as a low-allergen option and confirm preparation with staff.
The standard pork and beef curry sauces are wheat-based and are not gluten-free. Only the separately listed allergen-free curry is formulated without wheat.

The plant-based 'CoCo Ichi Veggie Curry' sauce uses no animal-derived ingredients, but dairy is flagged as present on shared factory production lines, so it is not suitable for those who must strictly avoid any dairy contact.

Veggie curry is available without advance reservation at any branch, which makes this Kawaramachi location a practical option for plant-based diners; confirm toppings, since standard toppings are not vegan.
CoCo Ichibanya publishes allergen, calorie, and ingredient-origin information, accessible via PDF and in-store QR codes, so diners can check specifics before ordering.
A genuinely useful feature for allergy-sensitive diners: the seven-allergen-free curry is delivered in a sealed pouch specifically to avoid kitchen cross-contact.
Both a low-allergen curry and a no-animal-ingredient veggie curry are on the standard menu chain-wide, available without booking ahead.

This is a wheat-flour bakery. The shop describes its breads as made from carefully selected ingredients centered on domestic wheat flour, so gluten is present throughout the kitchen and gluten-free or celiac-safe options should not be assumed. Flour dust and shared baking surfaces make cross-contamination effectively unavoidable in a working bakery of this kind.
No gluten-free product line or dedicated gluten-free preparation is documented in any source. Celiac and gluten-sensitive diners should confirm directly with the shop before eating.

Several breads lean on soy-based ingredients (soy cream, soy milk pudding, vegan mayo), so soy is a common allergen here even though it is a plant-based shop. No information is published on whether any seasonings contain wheat-based soy sauce; confirm with staff if you avoid wheat.

The entire bakery is 100% plant-based, with no animal-derived ingredients, no honey, and no refined white sugar processed with bone char, so there is no animal product on site to cross-contaminate vegan items.
Because the shop is fully vegan, there are no eggs, dairy, or animal products used anywhere, removing the usual cross-contact risks for vegan diners.
Fully vegan kitchen with a clear ingredient ethos: no animal products, no honey, and no bone-char-processed white sugar, which makes it a low-worry choice for strict vegan diners.
Bread is baked fresh daily in small batches and sold same-day, so ingredients and turnover are transparent and current.

The cafe advertises a vegan and gluten-free menu, with most dishes gluten-free and gluten-free options offered for the sandwich and burger. However, no source describes a dedicated gluten-free prep area, separate cookware, or cross-contamination controls, so celiac diners should confirm handling directly before ordering.

The ramen is offered in soy-sauce (shoyu) versions. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and no source confirms whether this kitchen uses a wheat-free tamari. Celiac and wheat-allergic diners should ask specifically whether the soy sauce used in the ramen and teriyaki burger is wheat-free.
The kitchen is fully vegan, so there is no animal-product cross-contact to worry about; the entire menu is plant-based.

The cafe takes reservations (reportedly in advance) and can accommodate special dietary requests, including avoiding particular ingredients for religious reasons. Diners are advised to flag ingredients to avoid when booking.
Fully plant-based menu with no alliums (onion, garlic, leek, chives, shallots), prepared along shojin ryori lines, making it well suited to vegans and to diners avoiding those ingredients.
Largely gluten-free menu with gluten-free options offered for the items that would normally contain gluten, such as the sandwich and burger.
Staff described as friendly and willing to accommodate dietary needs when given advance notice.
This is not a celiac-safe restaurant. The house specialty is gyoza, and standard gyoza wrappers are made from wheat flour; no gluten-free wrapper or dedicated gluten-free preparation is documented.

The kitchen also turns out battered/fried items such as karaage and kakiage (vegetable fritters), which use wheat flour and are typically cooked in shared oil, so cross-contamination with wheat is likely throughout the menu.

Gyoza here are served with soy- and vinegar-based dipping sauce and a miso-based dipping sauce. Standard Japanese soy sauce and miso commonly contain wheat, so these sauces should be assumed to contain gluten unless staff confirm otherwise.
This is a meat- and fish-forward gyoza izakaya, not set up for vegan dining. The signature gyoza are filled with pork/meat, and there is no documented vegan menu.

The miso dipping sauce is reported to contain fish powder (gyofun), so even vegetable dishes paired with the house sauces may carry animal-derived ingredients. Vegan diners should confirm each item directly.
The shop is small and owner-run, so the proprietress can answer questions about ingredients at the counter; diners describe a warm, personal atmosphere that makes it easy to ask.
Reviewers report the kitchen boils the gluten-free noodles separately in a dedicated gluten-free noodle pot and uses separate cooking ware for gluten-free orders.
Gluten-free ramen is served in a different-colored bowl to flag it as gluten-free, and place-setting markers are used to prevent mix-ups for gluten allergies.
This is not a dedicated gluten-free facility, and some reviewers note there is still a chance of cross-contamination in the shared kitchen.

A gluten-free travel writer chose not to dine here on her visit, citing caution about cross-contamination at non-dedicated ramen kitchens after being glutened at a ramen shop in Tokyo, though she noted it gets rave reviews and that she would likely try it next time.

Ramen seasonings and dashi in Japan commonly rely on soy sauce, most of which contains wheat. The shop emphasizes in-house soups and a wheat-free experience, but the specific soy sauce/tare used is not documented in these sources, so celiac diners should confirm the seasoning is wheat-free directly with staff.
Two clearly labeled vegan ramen options are offered and staff are described as knowledgeable about vegan accommodations.
Some users reported dishes labeled vegan that they felt weren't fully vegan, and that staff aren't always sure about every ingredient, so vegans should double-check specifics with staff.
Staff are repeatedly described as friendly, attentive to allergies, and as clearly understanding the needs of a celiac customer.

English-speaking staff and English menus with allergen information are available, and the kitchen is transparent about its limits (e.g., it can do pork-free chicken- or vegan-based bowls but cannot meet strict halal needs).
Some reviewers caution that staff are not always certain about every ingredient, so confirm specific allergen concerns directly.

Unlike most ramen shops, every bowl here can be made gluten-free using rice noodles (typically +200 yen, subject to stock), and the soups are prepared in-house with the stated goal of a wheat-free experience.
The shop was founded with celiac diners in mind because the owner's daughter has celiac disease, and reviewers generally report feeling safe and well cared for.
Concrete safety practices reported by diners include a separate pot for boiling gluten-free noodles, separate cooking ware, and different-colored bowls to distinguish gluten-free orders.
Gluten-free beer is available, a rare find at a ramen shop.
